description: We are a team of six Nanotechnology students passionate about space science, materials science, AI, and solving real-world challenges using NASA data. We aim to combine our scientific background with creative technology to build innovative, practical solutions. We are especially interested in materials, space safety, data analysis, and AI-driven systems.
summary:
Qamar Square is an educational space game built for NASA Space Apps’ “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer” challenge. Players act as a Junior Astronaut running a lunar base through real life-support emergencies during the 14-day lunar night: power loss, extreme cold, a failing oxygen generator, and a clogged water recycler. Every choice maps to a real NASA engineering option, explained simply as what it does, why it helps, and what can go wrong, so playing means learning how astronauts and engineers actually make these trade-offs.

The team researched each subsystem against 56 NASA Technical Reports Server publications, peer-reviewed papers, and agency program pages, then ran a scientific-verification pass to correct early drafts and label every technology by its true maturity: flight-proven, ground-tested, or lab research only. Four AI tools supported the work: Claude Code and Codex built the game, ChatGPT checked research against submission guidelines, and Gemini AI Plus supported the demo, which the team recorded manually from real gameplay. The result turns dense engineering trade-offs into an interactive mission trainer that is scientifically accurate and genuinely fun to play.
details:
Qamar Square is a 2D browser-based educational lunar survival game designed for children aged 7–12, inspired by NASA’s Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge. Players take on the role of junior mission commanders, responsible for managing a lunar base and keeping its crew safe until sunrise.

The game consists of four connected challenges: Power & Food, Heat & Shelter, Oxygen, and Water & Waste. Players make decisions while managing limited resources, and each decision can affect the availability of resources in subsequent challenges. Through this experience, players learn how essential lunar-base systems work and how they depend on one another. The game also includes simplified scientific explanations and real examples from space exploration to connect gameplay with real science.

Benefits and Intended Impact: The project makes complex space-related concepts easier and more engaging for children. It encourages scientific curiosity, critical thinking, problem-solving, resource management, and responsible decision-making. Its main impact is to introduce young learners to the challenges of lunar exploration and demonstrate the importance of sustainability and interconnected life-support systems in future space missions.

Tools and Technologies: The project was developed using JavaScript, HTML, CSS, and SVG. We used Vite as the development and build tool, Node.js for the development environment, GitHub for version control and collaboration, and Vercel for deployment. The game runs in a web browser and does not require specialized hardware.

Creativity and Innovation: Qamar Square combines educational gaming with a realistic lunar-survival scenario. Rather than teaching each system independently, it connects power, temperature, oxygen, water, and waste management through decisions that have consequences throughout the mission. It transforms scientific concepts into interactive challenges while maintaining an age-appropriate experience.

Factors Considered: Our team considered the target age group, scientific accuracy, accessibility, interface simplicity, limited resources, and the consequences of player decisions. We also considered how to simplify complex scientific information without losing its essential meaning, and how to make the game accessible on different devices while keeping its educational purpose central to the experience.
